mainTopic: What counts as birth when only the head or forehead emerges: שמואל's rule for a נפל is refuted, and ריש לקיש and רבי יוחנן disagree about the forehead and the firstborn's inheritance.
overview: The גמרא opens with שמואל: a נפל's head coming out does not count as its birth, because only a creature with 'breath of life in its nostrils' has a head that matters. The גמרא challenges him from our משנה, which uses the word 'ראשו' for a נפל. It first answers that the word means 'רובו' and was written only to match the next clause about a nine-month baby. That defense collapses, because the rule for a nine-month baby's head is already taught in חולין for animals and in נדה for humans. So the גמרא declares שמואל conclusively refuted. Next, ריש לקיש rules that a forehead coming out counts as birth everywhere except for the firstborn's inheritance, because the Torah says 'יכיר'. רבי יוחנן says it counts even for inheritance. The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן with sources that require seeing the nose to recognize a face. It answers by reading 'up to the nose,' and by explaining that testimony letting a woman remarry has a special rabbinic strictness about identifying the body. The עמוד ends as the גמרא begins a second answer, which continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: שמואל: The head of a non-viable fetus does not exempt
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that for a נפל, the emergence of the head alone does not count as birth to exempt the next child.
steps.simpleTranslation: The גמרא: שמואל said: The head does not exempt in the case of non-viable fetuses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with a rule from שמואל. If a נפל's head comes out, that does not count as its birth, so it does not exempt the next baby from פדיון הבן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a normal, viable baby, the head coming out counts as birth. שמואל says this is not true for a נפל. For a נפל, the head alone is not enough to make it the one that 'opened the womb' (פטר רחם).

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה
Exempts (here: exempts the next child from פדיון הבן)

steps.confusionAlert: שמואל is not saying a נפל can never exempt. The משנה teaches that a נפל does exempt from the כהן. He is only saying that the head of a נפל is not enough to count as its birth.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the whole סוגיא. It creates a difference between viable and non-viable births in what counts as 'being born.'

phrases.english: Gemara: Shmuel said:
The head does not exempt in the case of non-viable fetuses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For a נפל, the emergence of the head alone does not count as birth to exempt the next child from פדיון הבן.

steps.title: Asking for שמואל's source
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind שמואל's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where שמואל gets his rule from. This is a setup line, and the answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody is attacking שמואל here. The גמרא just wants to know why a נפל's head should be treated differently from a viable baby's head.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the rule in step 1
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The basis for treating a נפל's head as not counting.

steps.title: Only a living creature's head counts
steps.stepSummary: A פסוק about 'breath of life in its nostrils' teaches that only a viable creature's head is significant.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says: 'All in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life.' Wherever there is the breath of the spirit of life in its nostrils, its head is considered significant. Another (non-viable) one, its head is not considered significant.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק from the story of the flood. Life is connected to the nostrils, which are in the head, so the head is important only for a living, viable creature.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The head matters because it holds the 'breath of life.' A viable baby has that breath, so its head stands for the whole baby. A נפל is not viable, so its head has no special importance, and we need more of its body to come out.

keyTerms.meaning: Breath of the spirit of life
The other one (here: the non-viable fetus)

phrases.english: 'All in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life' —

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל הֵיכָא דְּנִשְׁמַת רוּחַ חַיִּים בְּאַפָּיו
phrases.english: wherever the breath of the spirit of life is in its nostrils,
that is where its head is considered significant;
the other one, its head is not considered significant.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֹּל אֲשֶׁר נִשְׁמַת רוּחַ חַיִּים בְּאַפָּיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק links life to the nostrils, so the head counts only for a viable creature.

steps.title: Challenge from the משנה's word 'its head'
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says a נפל 'whose head came out alive' exempts the next child, which seems to contradict שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: One who comes after non-viable fetuses, whose head came out alive, and a nine-month baby whose head came out dead. In any case, it teaches 'its head'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes our משנה to challenge שמואל. The משנה speaks about a נפל whose 'head' came out and treats that as enough to exempt the next child from the כהן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists the child born after a נפל as a בכור for inheritance but not for the כהן. That means the נפל already exempted him from פדיון. Since the משנה describes the נפל using 'ראשו' (its head), it looks like a נפל's head does count, against שמואל.

phrases.english: We learned: One who comes after non-viable fetuses,
whose head came out alive,
and a nine-month fetus whose head came out dead.
In any case, it teaches 'its head'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's rule from step 1
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's rule that a נפל's head does not exempt
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה uses 'ראשו' for a נפל and treats it as exempting the next child, so the head of a נפל seems to count.

steps.title: 'Its head' really means 'most of it'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that 'ראשו' in the משנה means 'רובו,' most of the body.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is 'its head'? Most of it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends שמואל. It reads the משנה's word 'ראשו' as meaning most of the body came out, not just the head.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If most of the נפל's body came out, everyone agrees that counts as birth. So the משנה is no longer talking about the head alone, and שמואל's rule stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Most of it (the majority of the body)

phrases.english: What is 'its head'?
Most of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 4
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting a word in the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'ראשו' means just the head, so a נפל's head counts.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'ראשו' means most of the body, so the משנה fits שמואל.

steps.title: Then why not say 'most of it'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה wrote 'ראשו' if it meant 'רובו.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let it teach 'most of it'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer. If the משנה meant 'most of it,' it should have written that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 5 is a stretch, because 'head' and 'most of the body' are different things. The גמרא wants a reason why the משנה would choose the less accurate word.

phrases.english: But let it teach 'most of it'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 5
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה should say exactly what it means. If it meant 'most,' it should have said 'most.'

steps.title: The first clause copies the wording of the second clause
steps.stepSummary: The משנה wrote 'ראשו' for the נפל to match the next clause about a nine-month baby. That clause says 'ראשו' so that we can infer the opposite case: if a viable baby's head came out alive, the head alone does count.
steps.simpleTranslation: By right, it should have taught 'most of it.' But since it needed to teach in the latter clause 'a nine-month fetus whose head came out dead' (the reason is that its head came out dead, but if its head came out alive, the one after it would not even be a firstborn for inheritance), it taught 'its head' in the first clause too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits the משנה really should have said 'רובו.' It explains that the משנה used 'ראשו' so the first case would match the wording of the second case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the second case, a viable nine-month baby, the משנה says 'ראשו מת' (which also means most of the body, Rashi) so that we can infer the opposite: if its head came out alive, it would already be the בכור, and the next child would lose even the inheritance. Since the סיפא had to say 'ראשו,' the תנא used the same word in the רישא for a smooth, matching style.
steps.whatToRemember: For now, the defense of שמואל is that the משנה's 'ראשו' for a נפל means 'רובו,' and was written as 'ראשו' only to match the סיפא about a nine-month baby. Steps 8–10 attack this defense, and step 11 concludes that שמואל is refuted.
steps.confusionAlert: The word 'ראשו' does not mean the head alone anywhere in the משנה, even in the סיפא: 'ראשו מת' there also means most of the body (Rashi). The משנה wrote 'ראשו' so we could infer the opposite case: if a viable baby's head came out alive, the head alone counts as birth.

phrases.aramaic: בְּדִין הוּא דְּאִיבְּעִי לֵיהּ לְמִיתְנֵי רוּבּוֹ,
phrases.english: By right, it should have taught 'most of it,'
but since it needed to teach in the latter clause
'a nine-month fetus whose head came out dead' —
the reason is that its head came out dead,
but if its head came out alive —

phrases.aramaic: הַבָּא אַחֲרָיו בְּכוֹר לַנַּחֲלָה נָמֵי לָא הָוֵי,
phrases.english: the one who comes after it would not be a firstborn for inheritance either,
so it taught 'its head' in the first clause as well.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּדִין הוּא דְּאִיבְּעִי לֵיהּ לְמִיתְנֵי רוּבּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6
steps.terutzResolutionType: Stylistic matching (אַיְּידֵי): the first clause borrows the wording of the second
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה should have written 'רובו' if that is what it meant.
steps.terutzMaskana: (Proposed) The משנה wrote 'ראשו' in the רישא only to match the סיפא, from which we infer that a viable baby's head truly counts when it comes out alive, so שמואל's rule would stand. Steps 8–10 undo this, because the סיפא turns out to be redundant.

steps.title: The nine-month clause seems to teach nothing new
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the nine-month clause adds, since we already learned that when a head comes out, it counts as birth.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is the משנה teaching us? That once the baby puts out its head, it counts as born? We already learned this: 'If it put out its head, even though it pulled it back in, it is considered born!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 7. It argues that the משנה's next clause, which says the head counts for a nine-month baby, is unnecessary, because another משנה already teaches this rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 depended on the nine-month clause being a real, necessary teaching. If that clause just repeats a known rule from חולין, the משנה would have no reason to write it. Then it also had no reason to use the word 'ראשו' to match it. That would bring back the problem for שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it teaching us? (a challenge that a ruling seems to add nothing new)

phrases.english: And what is it teaching us?
That once it puts out its head
it counts as a birth?
We already learned: If it put out its head,
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה in חולין 68a, which is about an animal fetus.

phrases.english: even though it pulled it back in,
it is considered born!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer in step 7 by claiming that the clause it relied on is redundant.
steps.kashyaTarget: The nine-month clause of the משנה, which step 7 used to explain the word 'ראשו'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rule that a head coming out counts as birth is already stated in the משנה in חולין. So this clause adds nothing, and it cannot justify the wording.

steps.title: Maybe one source is for animals and one is for humans
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the חולין source covers animals and our משנה covers humans. It explains why neither case could be learned from the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say: there it taught us about an animal, and here it teaches us about a human. This is needed because a human cannot be learned from an animal, since an animal has no hidden opening. And an animal cannot be learned from a human, because a human's face is important.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a possible defense: maybe both sources are needed, one for animals and one for humans. It explains why each case is different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For an animal, the womb's opening is not hidden between its thighs (Rashi), so the head coming out is easy to see and counts as birth. We might not apply that to a woman, where the opening is hidden. In the other direction, a human face is especially important (חשיב פרצוף פנים דידיה), so a human's head may count as birth for that reason alone. So a rule about humans might not apply to animals. Because of these differences, both sources would be needed.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you say (introduces a possible answer)
Hidden opening or corridor (the hidden entrance to the womb)

steps.confusionAlert: This answer is only a suggestion. The words 'וכי תימא' mean 'if you would say.' The very next step shows that this answer does not work.

phrases.english: And if you say: it taught us about an animal,
and here it teaches us about a human,
since a human cannot be learned from an animal,
because it (the animal) has no hidden opening.
phrases.notes: For an animal, the head coming out is plainly visible.

phrases.english: And an animal cannot be learned from a human,
because his (the human's) face is important.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a possible defense against step 8 by showing that both sources are needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: both sources are needed because animals and humans are different
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The nine-month clause is redundant because חולין already teaches that the head counts as birth.
steps.terutzMaskana: (Proposed) חולין teaches the rule for animals, and our משנה teaches it for humans.

steps.title: The rule for humans is also already taught
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the defense, because a משנה in נדה already teaches that a human baby counts as born once most of its head comes out.
steps.simpleTranslation: We already learned this too: 'If it came out in the normal way, it counts as born once most of its head comes out. And what is most of its head? Once its forehead comes out.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the defense from step 9. It points to a משנה in נדה that already gives this rule for humans.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if we need separate sources for animals and humans, both of those sources already exist: חולין for animals and נדה for humans. So the nine-month clause in our משנה still adds nothing new. That means it cannot be the reason the משנה wrote 'ראשו' for the נפל.

phrases.english: This too we already learned:
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה in נדה 28a, which is about humans.

phrases.english: If it came out in its normal way,
it counts as born once most of its head comes out.
And what is most of its head?
Once its forehead comes out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the defense in step 9, so the challenge from step 8 stands again.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that our משנה is the source for the rule about humans.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The rule for humans already appears in the משנה in נדה, so our משנה's clause would still be redundant.

steps.title: שמואל is conclusively refuted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that שמואל's position is decisively refuted.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is a refutation of שמואל, a conclusive refutation!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the discussion and declares that שמואל's view has been disproven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The nine-month clause has been shown to be redundant, so it cannot explain why the משנה wrote 'ראשו.' That means 'ראשו' in the נפל clause really means the head. So the head of a נפל does count, which goes against שמואל's teaching that only a viable creature's head is significant.

keyTerms.meaning: A refutation, a decisive disproof of an אמורא's view

steps.whatToRemember: Every attempt to read 'ראשו' in our משנה as 'רובו' failed. So the head of a נפל does count to exempt the next child, and שמואל is refuted.
steps.whyThisMatters: The word 'תיובתא' in the גמרא means the view is rejected as הלכה.

phrases.english: A refutation of שמואל,
a conclusive refutation!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Once the defense collapses, the challenge from step 4 stands, and the גמרא declares the refutation.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: שמואל's view is refuted. The משנה's 'ראשו' for a נפל means the actual head.

steps.title: A forehead counts as birth except for inheritance
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש rules that when a baby's forehead comes out, it counts as born for all laws except the firstborn's inheritance, because the Torah requires 'recognition.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן לקיש said: When the forehead comes out, it counts as birth in every area of law, except for inheritance. Why? Because the Torah says 'he shall recognize' the firstborn.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new statement from רבי שמעון בן לקיש about a baby whose forehead comes out first. He says this counts as birth everywhere except for the firstborn's double share of the inheritance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, once the forehead emerges, the baby counts as 'born,' so a twin born after it cannot be a בכור for redemption. The firstborn's double portion is different, because the פסוק says 'יכיר' and a forehead alone is not enough to recognize who the child is. So for נחלה, the twin whose face comes out first is the בכור (Rashi).

keyTerms.meaning: Exempts. Here it means it counts as the birth, so the next child is not a firstborn for redemption.
Inheritance; here, the firstborn's double portion
'He shall recognize' (דברים כא:יז), the verse about the firstborn's double share
'The Merciful One.' A name for God, used when quoting the Torah.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the forehead 'doesn't count' at all. It does count as birth everywhere. Inheritance is the one exception, because of the special word יכיר.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said:
The forehead exempts (counts as birth) in all cases,
phrases.notes: If the forehead comes out first, a twin born after it is not a firstborn for the כהן.

phrases.english: except for inheritance.
What is the reason?
The Merciful One said 'he shall recognize,'
phrases.notes: A forehead alone is not enough to recognize the child.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic after the refutation of שמואל: what counts as birth when only the forehead emerges.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Emergence of the forehead counts as birth for all laws except the firstborn's inheritance, which needs facial recognition (יכיר).

steps.title: A forehead counts even for inheritance
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן disagrees and says the forehead counts as birth even for the firstborn's inheritance.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: Even for inheritance, the forehead counts.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives the opposing view. For him, the forehead counts as birth even for the double inheritance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן holds that the forehead is enough even for the inheritance law, with no exception. He evidently does not read יכיר as requiring the whole face with the nose. That is exactly what the coming challenges will attack.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:
Even for inheritance.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The opposing side of the מחלוקת with ריש לקיש.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The forehead counts as birth even for the firstborn's inheritance.

steps.title: What does 'in all cases' include?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what extra case ריש לקיש meant to include with the words 'in all cases.'
steps.simpleTranslation: 'In all cases': what does this come to include?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question about the words of ריש לקיש. It is setting up the next step, which names the specific case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'בכל מקום' sound broad. The גמרא wants a concrete case besides בכורה where the forehead counts as birth.

keyTerms.meaning: In all cases; in every area
'To include what?' A question asking what extra case a phrase adds.

phrases.english: 'In all cases.' What does it come to include?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the wording of ריש לקיש's statement in step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which additional case is included by 'בכל מקום'?

steps.title: The convert whose baby's forehead came out before she converted
steps.stepSummary: It includes a convert whose baby's forehead came out while she was still a non-Jew. The baby counts as born before her conversion, so she has no birth-related purity laws or offering.
steps.simpleTranslation: It includes what the Rabbis taught: A convert whose baby's forehead came out while she was still a non-Jew, and only afterward she converted. We do not give her the days of impurity and days of purity, and she does not bring a birth offering.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. 'In all cases' includes the case of a גיורת whose baby's forehead came out before she converted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the forehead counts as birth, the birth happened before the conversion, when she was not yet Jewish. So the laws of a Jewish woman after birth do not apply to her: the ימי טומאה, the ימי טהרה, and the קרבן לידה.

keyTerms.meaning: Her state as a non-Jew, before converting
The days of impurity and purity a woman counts after giving birth
The offering a woman brings after giving birth

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the forehead rule is not just about בכורה. It sets the actual moment of birth for other laws too.

phrases.english: To include that which the Rabbis taught:
A convert whose child's forehead came out while she was a non-Jew,
and afterward she converted:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין נוֹתְנִין לָהּ יְמֵי טוּמְאָה וִימֵי טׇהֳרָה,
phrases.english: we do not give her days of impurity and days of purity,
and she does not bring a birth offering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It includes the convert whose baby's forehead emerged before her conversion. The birth is counted from that moment, so she has no post-birth purity laws or offering.

steps.title: A ברייתא says recognition needs the face with the nose
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן from a ברייתא that defines יכיר as recognizing the face together with the nose.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: 'He shall recognize' means recognizing the face. And what is recognizing the face? The face together with the nose.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי יוחנן with a ברייתא. The ברייתא says the 'recognition' the Torah requires means seeing the face including the nose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If יכיר requires the face with the nose, then a forehead alone is not enough for inheritance. That supports ריש לקיש and contradicts רבי יוחנן.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
'He shall recognize': this is recognition of the face,
and what is recognition of the face?
The features of the face with the nose.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן's view from step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that the forehead counts even for inheritance
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא defines יכיר as recognizing the face with the nose. A forehead alone does not meet that standard.

steps.title: Read it as 'up to the nose'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the reading of the ברייתא to 'up to the nose,' meaning the nose itself is not needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Teach it as: 'up to the nose.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי יוחנן by rereading the ברייתא. It does not say 'with the nose' but 'up to the nose.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: With this reading, recognition only needs the upper face, above the nose. So the forehead area can be enough, and רבי יוחנן's view stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Up to the nose, but not including it

steps.confusionAlert: 'Up to the nose' means the nose is NOT included. Only the part above it is needed.

phrases.english: Teach: 'up to the nose.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא requires the nose for recognition.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא reads 'up to the nose,' so the nose is not required.

steps.title: Testimony about a dead man requires the nose
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה: witnesses can identify a dead husband only if they saw his face with the nose.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: People may testify only on the features of the face with the nose.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second challenge to רבי יוחנן. This one comes from the laws of identifying a dead man so his wife may remarry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here too the source says 'with the nose' is needed to identify a person. That suggests real recognition needs the nose, against רבי יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: Testify; here, witnesses who identify a dead man so his wife may remarry

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין מְעִידִים אֶלָּא עַל פַּרְצוּף פָּנִים עִם הַחוֹטֶם.
phrases.english: One may testify only on the features of the face with the nose.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: אֵין מְעִידִים אֶלָּא עַל פַּרְצוּף פָּנִים עִם הַחוֹטֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new source with the same challenge, after step 17's answer.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Identifying a person requires the nose. So 'recognition' should need the nose, and a forehead alone should not count.

steps.title: Again, read it as 'up to the nose'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives the same answer: reread the משנה as 'up to the nose.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Teach: 'up to the nose.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the second challenge the same way as the first, by rereading the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once again, the nose is not needed, only the face above it. So this source no longer contradicts רבי יוחנן.

phrases.english: Teach: 'up to the nose.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 18.
steps.terutzMaskana: Testimony requires the face only up to the nose.

steps.title: A source that clearly requires the nose, with a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says witnesses need both the forehead and the face, together with the nose. אביי (or רב כהנא) brings a פסוק showing that recognition includes the nose.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If they saw the forehead without the face, or the face without the forehead, they cannot testify until they see both, with the nose. And אביי said (some say רב כהנא): What is the verse? 'The recognition of their faces testifies against them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third and stronger challenge to רבי יוחנן. This source clearly requires the nose and backs it with a פסוק about 'recognition.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here 'up to the nose' cannot work, because the source lists both forehead and face and still adds 'with the nose.' The פסוק 'הכרת פניהם' uses the same idea of recognition as 'יכיר.' So it seems that recognition by Torah standards needs the nose, and a forehead alone should not count for inheritance.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What is the verse?' Asking for the scriptural source.
'The recognition of their faces testifies against them' (ישעיהו ג:ט)

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A forehead without the features of the face,
the features of the face without the forehead:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין מְעִידִין עַד שֶׁיְּהוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עִם הַחוֹטֶם.
phrases.english: they may not testify until both are seen, with the nose.
And Abaye said, and some say Rav Kahana:
What is the verse?
'The recognition of their faces testifies against them'!
phrases.notes: By this פסוק's standard, recognizing a face includes the nose.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: פַּדַּחַת בְּלֹא פַּרְצוּף פָּנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A stronger challenge that the 'up to the nose' rereading cannot answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that the forehead counts for inheritance
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The source explicitly needs forehead, face, and nose, and grounds it in a פסוק about recognition. So recognition (יכיר) should need the nose too.

steps.title: Testimony for a woman is stricter
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that testimony allowing a woman to remarry is special, because the Rabbis made it stricter.
steps.simpleTranslation: Testimony for a woman is different, because the Rabbis were strict about it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי יוחנן by limiting the challenge. The nose requirement comes from a special rabbinic strictness for testimony that lets a woman remarry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra need for the nose is a חומרא of the Rabbis, because a mistake could lead to an אשת איש remarrying. It does not define what 'recognition' means for the firstborn's inheritance. So for בכורה and נחלה, the forehead can still be enough, as רבי יוחנן says.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is different.' This introduces a distinction.
Testimony that a husband died, allowing his wife to remarry

steps.whatToRemember: ריש לקיש: the forehead counts as birth everywhere except the firstborn's inheritance, which needs יכיר. רבי יוחנן: it counts even for inheritance. The challenges are answered by reading 'up to the nose,' and by explaining that testimony for a woman to remarry has a special rabbinic strictness.

phrases.english: Testimony for a woman is different,
since the Rabbis were stringent with it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The nose requirement defines Torah-level recognition and applies to inheritance too.
steps.terutzMaskana: The nose requirement is a rabbinic חומרא only for testimony letting a woman remarry. For inheritance, the forehead suffices.

steps.title: Were the Rabbis really strict? They were lenient in this testimony
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the claim that the Rabbis were stricter with testimony for a woman to remarry. A משנה shows they accepted even weak kinds of witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: Were the Rabbis really strict here? But we learned in a משנה that the Rabbis set the practice of letting a woman remarry based on a witness repeating what another witness said. They also accepted the word of a woman, a slave, or a maidservant!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 21. It brings a משנה showing that the Rabbis were actually lenient, not strict, with testimony that lets a woman remarry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 21 said that seeing the nose is needed because the Rabbis made this testimony stricter. Normally, though, hearsay, a woman, and a slave cannot testify, and here the Rabbis accept all of them. That looks like the opposite of strictness, so the reason given in step 21 seems to fall apart.

keyTerms.meaning: And were they really strict? (an opening that challenges)
But we learned in a משנה (brings a source to contradict)
They established as a set practice
Allowing a woman to marry again
A witness repeating what another witness told him (hearsay)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the משנה means the Rabbis do not care about this testimony. The leniency is about WHO may testify. The next step shows that the strictness is about something else.

phrases.english: And were they really strict?
phrases.notes: This question is really a challenge to what was said in step 21.

phrases.english: But we learned in a משנה:
phrases.notes: The source is משנה יבמות קכב.

phrases.english: They established the practice of allowing a woman to remarry
phrases.notes: Based on the kinds of testimony listed next.

phrases.english: based on a witness reporting from another witness,
phrases.notes: Hearsay, which is normally not accepted.

phrases.aramaic: מִפִּי אִשָּׁה, מִפִּי עֶבֶד, מִפִּי שִׁפְחָה!
phrases.english: from a woman, from a slave, from a maidservant!
phrases.notes: All of these are normally not valid witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in step 21, that the Rabbis were stricter.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 21 that testimony for a woman to remarry is stricter.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The Rabbis accept witnesses here who are normally invalid. That shows leniency, which contradicts the claim of strictness.

steps.title: Lenient about reporting the death, but not about identifying the body
steps.stepSummary: The Rabbis were lenient about who may report the death. They were not lenient about how carefully the dead man must be identified.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the Rabbis were lenient, it was about the end of the testimony. About its beginning, the Rabbis were not lenient.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by splitting the testimony into two parts: identifying the body, and reporting the death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'end' is the report that the husband died, and here even hearsay or a woman is accepted. The 'beginning' is the actual recognition of the dead man, and there the Rabbis stay strict, so the nose must be seen. Both rules can be true at the same time, so step 21's answer still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: At its end (the report of the death)

steps.whatToRemember: In testimony for a woman to remarry, the Rabbis were lenient about who reports the death. They were strict about properly identifying the dead man, which includes seeing the nose.
steps.whyThisMatters: This two-part split is a basic tool for understanding the laws of עדות אשה. Being lenient in one part does not mean being lenient in every part.

phrases.english: When the Rabbis were lenient, it was at its end,
phrases.notes: "Its end" means who may report that the husband died.

phrases.english: at its beginning the Rabbis were not lenient.
phrases.notes: "Its beginning" means how carefully the body must be identified.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אַקִּילוּ רַבָּנַן בְּסוֹפָהּ, בִּתְחִלָּתָהּ לָא אַקִּילוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 22 and saves the answer from step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction between two stages of the same testimony
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the Rabbis accept weak witnesses, they must be lenient about this testimony in every way.
steps.terutzMaskana: The leniency covers only who reports the death. Identifying the body stays strict, so the nose is required.

steps.title: Opening a second possible answer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא signals that it will now give a different answer to the earlier difficulty.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say instead:
steps.whatsHappening: This is only a setup line. The גמרא is getting ready to give a second answer, which comes in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'ואיבעית אימא' means the first answer was fine, but here is another way to solve the same problem. The content of the new answer has not been said yet. It continues on the next עמוד: the יכיר of inheritance and recognizing a face for testimony are two separate standards.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say instead (introduces another answer)

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
phrases.notes: Here comes another answer, and it continues on the next עמוד.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces a second answer to the difficulty from step 20, alongside the answer in steps 21 and 23.
steps.terutzMaskana: The answer comes at the top of 47a: the יכיר of inheritance and recognizing a face for testimony are two separate standards.
